SEC-HC-03.note: A is a bare comma splice, B and D are obvious fragments; only one option is a sentence. Same conjunctive-adverb frame as 01 ('; however,').

SEC-HC-05.note: Resolved partly by the words after the blank: 'kitchenware, and a location' shows the list is comma-separated, which kills A's semicolon.

SEC-HC-06.note: C is B minus 'remarkable' plus a comma: the near-twin distractor is the shorter one, a length tell. Colon in B is acceptable but a semicolon would be the more natural mark; the second clause is an instance, not an explanation.

SEC-HC-07.note: B and C begin with ', ' after a blank that already follows a space; if rendered literally ('cores , which') the typography tips a reader off before grammar does.

SEC-HC-08.note: 'its proportions' after the blank quietly confirms the singular subject; C (compound subject + plural verb) fails only on the comma before 'remain', which strong students will weigh.

SEC-HC-09.note: Ambiguous stem. D is the only option with no mechanical fault, but it makes the whose-clause restrictive on an already-definite 'The strait's array'. A has the natural nonrestrictive commas and fails only on 'array of turbines produce' -- notional plural agreement with 'an array of' is widely attested (like 'a number of') and many editors would pass it. The category label ('nonrestrictive addition, with agreement') suggests A may even be the intended key. Either way two options survive; needs a rewrite so that the commas and the verb agree in one option.

SEC-HC-10.note: Appositive 'an element the surrounding limestone lacks' right after the blank cues the comma; the agreement half is the only work left.

SEC-HC-12.note: 'Each of ... has' is textbook; C drops 'with age' (length tell) and D is A with a dash. Effectively a two-option item.

SEC-HC-14.note: B ('Since ... were first photographed in the 1930s, scholars ... consistently found') is grammatical if 'since' is read causally rather than temporally; the reading is strained by context but not ungrammatical. Weak flag.

SEC-HC-15.note: D 'had already showed': Merriam-Webster and AHD list 'showed' as an acceptable (less common) past participle, so D is defensible under a recognised dictionary convention. Replace D with a genuinely wrong form (e.g. 'have already showed' or 'would already show').

SEC-HC-16.note: Cued by the word immediately after the blank: 'trained' needs a subject, so who/whom is decided before the parenthetical 'the guild's own records say' is even parsed. A remains a strong hypercorrection trap.

SEC-HC-17.note: Cued by 'had first noticed' immediately after the blank (subject needed -> who). Third who/whom item in a row whose key is the subject form.

SEC-HC-18.note: 'could' after the four-word interrupter resolves whoever/whomever; all three pronoun-case items (16-18) key to the subject form, so 'whom is never right' solves the block.

SEC-HC-19.note: Verb after the blank ('predicts') eliminates the number twin; the remaining two are fragment/expletive shapes shared with 20 and 21.

SEC-HC-20.note: Same option template as 19 and 21: singular NP, plural NP, 'which'-fragment, expletive/prepositional dangler. 'survive' after the blank picks the number.

SEC-HC-21.note: Same option template as 19 and 20; 'preserves' after the blank picks the number, and the plain NP is the key in all three.

SEC-HC-24.note: D ('had to detect, distinguish, and to relay') is faulty parallelism under Chicago/Garner (repeat 'to' on all or none) but is the one distractor a strong student will pause on. 'the whole sequence must finish' after the blank forces the semicolon and kills C.
